source.title: Asymmetric Scaling Laws from Sparse Features

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper theoretically analyzes and experimentally measures scaling in a synthetic sparse random-feature model, rather than reproducing language-model pretraining experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own population-loss scaling, compute-allocation, scaling-collapse, and double-descent results for synthetic linear and ReLU random-feature models. Statements about other papers' results in the introduction and related work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a solvable toy-model theory paper. Every result comes from a frozen random-feature map with a trained linear readout, on synthetic sparse Bernoulli/power-law regression data with squared loss. Its systems are not language models, nor image, video or fine-tuned neural models, so no row measures what a version names in the same kind of system. The paper offers a mechanism (sparse feature coverage) that could explain unequal N and D exponents and a data-heavy compute split. It does not measure whether V3, V5 or V7 hold for real models. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version instead of as verdicts.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also prove high-probability GD stability for step sizes below 2. They derive a power-law scaling for the probability that GD diverges from rare activation spikes, and suggest gradient clipping as a remedy. They frame the takeaway as sparsity shaping scaling in high-dimensional learning. Testing in transformers and at scale is left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a synthetic sparse random-feature regression model, population/test squared loss, and sweeps of parameters and examples; it does not use language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted exponents differ between sparse and dense sweeps and between linear and ReLU feature maps. The paper also states that solver-dependent compute models can change the compute exponent while preserving the balanced parameter/data allocation.

fits_no_version.finding: In a sparse random-feature regression toy model, loss follows two exponents: αN=α1+α2+1 and αD=(α1+α2+1)/(α1+1). This was verified empirically (linear: 2.0 joint vs 1.11; ReLU: 1.25 vs 1.10, and 1.5 vs 1.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse input activation can make data-limited and model-limited loss exponents differ in solvable random-feature models.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a proxy compute C=N·D·min{N,D}, the toy model's compute-optimal allocation is N*∼C^(1/(α1+3)) and D*∼C^((α1+1)/(α1+3)), favouring data as sparsity grows. Empirical curves approach the predicted frontier.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data sparsity shifts the compute-optimal allocation toward data in toy regression models.

fits_no_version.finding: Rescaled loss collapses onto a universal curve, with a ridgeless double-descent peak at the K(D)=N threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toy random-feature loss obeys a scale-invariant collapse with a sparsity-located interpolation peak.

record.problems: The evidence is from a synthetic regression model, not language models. The nonlinear results are experimental rather than a theoretical treatment. The gradient-descent failure-probability experiment is explicitly described as unable to reach the asymptotic predicted exponent with its available sample sizes; this result is outside the listed claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out. Cited results from other work were not recorded.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss is measured.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No measured compute-optimal N and D for neural models; only an analytic toy derivation.
No depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer neural models.
No comparison of fitting or setup choices on real model scaling laws.

missing.what: GD divergence-probability scaling: P(diverge) falls from 0.370 at D=500 to <0.00025 at D=10,000. Local exponents reach about 4.5, short of the predicted 9. This bears on no version but is the paper's own scaling law.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests' and T2 classification is overridden. A synthetic linear-readout regression toy model is not the kind of system the versions describe, so it gives no verdicts on V3, V5 or V7. Its relevance is as a theoretical mechanism for asymmetric exponents and a data-favouring allocation.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy in language models; its experiments use population/test squared loss in synthetic regression models.
It does not report a prediction from power-law fits on small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger. Its scaling-collapse result is not such a small-run extrapolation test.
The compute-optimal result is for a synthetic random-feature model with dataset size measured in examples and a stated proxy compute budget, not language-model tokens or LLM training.
The paper compares linear and ReLU feature maps but does not measure the effect of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count as stated in this version.
The paper tests synthetic sparse-feature regression, including a ReLU feature map; it does not test image/video modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The paper varies sparsity, feature map, and compute model, but does not test parameter-counting conventions, language-model training schedules, or the effects of alternative fitting procedures on published LLM exponents.

rows.subject: sparse random-feature model
rows.size_stated: N and D vary; specific sweep values not stated in the main-text compute-frontier figure description
rows.operation_detail: Derive the compute-optimal allocation under C = N D · min{N, D}; compare loss-versus-compute curves with the predicted frontier.

conditions.value: compute-optimal allocation lies in N < D

rows.measure: Optimal N, D and loss as powers of compute
rows.value: N*(C) ∼ C^(1/(α1+3)); D*(C) ∼ C^((α1+1)/(α1+3)); ℓ*(C) ∼ C^(-(α1+α2+1)/(α1+3)). Empirical curves approach the predicted frontier at high compute.
rows.locator: Section 5, Proposition 5.1 and Figure 3; Appendix D.3
rows.note: This is a theoretical result with an empirical frontier comparison. Appendix D states that alternative solver costs can change the compute exponent while retaining the loss-balanced allocation D ∼ N^(α1+1).
rows.check: The allocation exponents come from an analytic derivation under a proxy compute C=N·D·min{N,D}. The only empirical evidence is a figure showing curves 'approach' the frontier, with no fitted N* or D* exponents. This is not a measurement of LM compute-optimal allocation, so it is not a V3 test.

rows.subject: sparse random-feature model

rows.operation_detail: Rescale loss and parameter/data ratio across multiple N,D pairs and examine the loss curve.
rows.measure: Rescaled population loss and double-descent peak
rows.baseline: Two-regime power-law asymptotes: ℓ ∼ N^-(α1+α2+1) and ℓ ∼ D^(-(α1+α2+1)/(α1+1))
rows.value: Curves collapse onto a universal rescaled function; a prominent double-descent peak appears near the interpolation threshold ξcrit
rows.note: The paper describes the collapse and peak in text; it also notes that regularization or early stopping smooths the peak.
rows.check: Scaling collapse and double-descent peak in ridgeless toy regression. The paper itself says the peak comes from ridgeless interpolation, not from the scaling-law picture, and that regularization smooths it. This is not evidence that LM loss curves bend away from a power law (V7).
